title: The Will to Teach: How the Five Key Beliefs Apply to Teachers (and What Admin Can Do to Help!) min-can-do-to-help
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. extends his Five Key Beliefs framework—originally developed for student motivation—to the professional motivational lives of teachers, arguing that the same four belief categories (Credibility, Value, Effort/Efficacy, and Belonging) map cleanly onto the common sources of teacher demotivation. He identifies four buckets of teacher motivational problems—problems with leadership, problems with the idea of teaching, problems with the actual practice of teaching, and problems with perceived fit—and maps each to a tier of the Five Key Beliefs pyramid. The piece offers concrete strategies from The Will to Learn that administrators can deploy to cultivate each belief in their teachers, from tracking MGCs and modeling gentle urgency for Credibility, to delivering mini-sermons and providing knowledge feasts for Value, to Woodenization and defining success for Effort/Efficacy. Stuart Jr. concludes that great leadership resembles great teaching in its orientation toward the motivational inner lives of its charges, and that the capacity to influence teacher beliefs is both learnable and consequential.
points: Teacher demotivation maps precisely to the Five Key Beliefs: leadership problems signal Credibility issues, perceived meaninglessness signals Value deficits, persistent failure signals Effort/Efficacy problems, and a sense of not fitting in signals Belonging problems.

Administrators can build Credibility with teachers through the same strategies teachers use with students: tracking MGCs, improving targeted competencies one at a time, and demonstrating gentle urgency.

Admins address Value by delivering mini-sermons that speak to teachers' real doubts about the worth of their work, and by providing a feast of professional knowledge that deepens teachers' sense of what can be learned in the field.
Woodenization — explicit modeling of expected behaviors — benefits teachers as much as students; leaders who show and tell and model produce more capable colleagues than those who merely exhort.

Struggle normalization addresses Belonging not through lip service but by demonstrating that the struggles a teacher faces are shared by colleagues they perceive as stronger — an experience that must be engineered, not just announced.
quotes: Teachers, like students, are souls, and at the center of those souls sits a volitional core. Here — in the spirit, the heart, the executive center of our being — there exists a little garden from which motivation will grow, with a power like Jack's beanstalk, when given the right conditions.

Great leadership is a lot like great teaching in that it requires that the leader take seriously the doubts teachers have about these Five Key Belief areas. If you don't attend to these with a genuine and intelligent concern, your teachers will be left to grapple with them on their own.

Good leaders (just like good teachers) cast frequent and crystal clear visions of success. They also lead their teachers in exercises that let them define success, too (e.g., Everest Statement exercises).

Struggle normalization isn't about throwaway lip service to how hard teaching is. It's about demonstrating that certain struggles are common, that folks we perceive as better at their jobs than us also struggle with the same things we do.

That's a fair enough idea, but is it a good one? If we can do things — fairly simple and learnable things — that reliably help students to care more, then isn't it just common sense to get really good at doing those kinds of things?
Woodenization is basically all about high quality, efficient, direct instruction — you're showing and telling and modeling how to do a thing.
